Skip to main content Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Robotics arXiv:2610.22471 (cs) [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026] Title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence? Authors: SenseNova , Joint Research Team : Zhongang Cai , Ziang Cao , Tailai Chen , Han Chong Chua , Linjun Dai , Hanming Deng , Hokin Deng , Haiwen Diao , Chenjing Ding , Weichen Fan , Xiao Fu , Zerui Gong , Chenyang Gu , Zexin He , Zhi Hou , Bo Li , Qinyue Li , Quanzhou Li , Xiaowan Li , Zhichao Liao , Dahua Lin , Zilong Lin , Bo Liu , Chunxiao Liu , Pengfei Liu , Tianqi Liu , Ziwei Liu , Chen Change Loy , Lewei Lu , Jiapeng Luo , Yuexiao Ma , Liang Pan , Xingang Pan , Oscar Qian , Ziyi Shang , Yuyao Shao , Dawei Su , Dacheng Tao , Qingyi Tao , Quan Wang , Ruisi Wang , Xiaogang Wang , Ziyi Wang , Beichen Wen , Donghao Wu , Jiaxu Wu , Silei Wu , Xiaoming Wu , Zhonghua Wu , Hongcan Xiao , Weiye Xu , Atsushi Yamashita , Lei Yang , Zhe Yang , Baiqiao Yin , Wanqi Yin , Hanfei Zhao , Tianbo Zhong , Long Zhuo , Jing Zuo View a PDF of the paper titled Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?, by SenseNova and Joint Research Team: Zhongang Cai and 59 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., {\pi}0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence. live_web_research.page_text: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence? · Technical Report Skip to content Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence? Embodied competence — largely yes . Practical embodied intelligence — not yet . We ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field: we probe its limits on 12 benchmarks, dissect the harness behind it, validate it on eight real-robot platforms, and prototype what the next generation of embodied benchmarks should measure. Technical report ↗ Code ↗ Packages ↗ Logs ↗ GPT-6-Astra 01 Study 12 benchmarks 02 Harness ablation 03 Real World 8 platforms 04 Prototype next generation 01 · Empirical Study Large-Scale Study under a Unified Protocol Probing the capability upper bound of GPT-6-Astra across 12 benchmarks Sort by result Sort by gain over SOTA Group by embodiment GPT-6-Astra under a protocol that allows in-context learning on the training set and extends the execution budget up to 10×. Published baselines are reported under the standard budget, collected as of October 12, 2026. * Result with a VLA model. ‡ Zero-shot, without access to training data. In-context learning protocol ICL In-context learning from the training set Successful demonstrations are conventionally accessible when training smaller task-specific policies, so GPT-6-Astra may use them too. It studies the training data and builds a frozen knowledge package of task guidance, motion and visual references, executable helpers, recovery procedures and metadata, then retrieves and adapts these resources to each test scene. 10× A substantially larger execution budget We allow up to 10× the official step limit, since standard step limits can significantly underestimate GPT-6-Astra. Its emerging capability for failure recovery lets it translate additional steps into higher success, nearly saturating SIMPLE and the LIBERO family. Extensions continue the same episode — no resets. In-context learning: what GPT-6-Astra keeps Contents of an ICL knowledge package Knowledge package K written by GPT-6-Astra during ICL preparation · frozen before testing Task guidance goals, stages, strategies .md Motion references trajectories, grasps, phase anchors .npz Visual references demo frames, contact crops .png Executable helpers FK / IK, retrieval, action generation .py Checks & recovery completion tests, failure fixes .md .py Metadata & provenance robot specs, sources, validation .md .py read Test episode GPT-6 retrieve · adapt · check observations + robot states Success rate versus step budget Success rate versus step budget. The budget is expressed as a multiple of each benchmark's official step limit; dots show observed success rates and pink curves show fitted trends. We evaluate budgets up to 10× the official limit (1× for BEHAVIOR). The gray line marks the upper bound, which assumes that every episode that exhausts the evaluated budget without succeeding has the potential to succeed with an unlimited budget. Limitations and failure modes ← 1 / 5 → 1 Limitation Task-specific ICL 2 Limitation Time & cost 3 Failure mode Verifying physical success 4 Failure mode Consequential actions 5 Failure mode Progress over long horizons Limitation ICL packages are largely task-specific, which limits transfer Packages are built from each benchmark's training data, so their benefit weakens once test tasks move away from it. Packages that generalize beyond their source tasks remain an open direction . RoboDojo · Open group Lowest SR No task-specific demonstrations; it relies on a package studied from the other four groups. GPT-6-Astra + ICL still benefits from more interaction, but attains the lowest success of all groups. RoboLab · no training set 69.2 % No task-level package can be built (zero-shot, 10× budget). GPT-6-Astra leads the best listed baseline (42.9%), yet its absolute success remains moderate. Close coverage >95 % Where test tasks follow the training distribution — LIBERO family, SIMPLE, VLN-CE — demonstrated motions or routes are retrieved almost directly and success approaches saturation: above 95% on the LIBERO family and SIMPLE, around 90% on VLN-CE at 10×. SIMPLE · zero-shot → ICL 70.8 → 90.8 % Standard-budget success on the four common tasks, with shorter successful episodes under ICL. Limitation Time and cost remain high Even nearly solved benchmarks are expensive: about 1M tokens and nearly an hour per LIBERO-Long++ episode, roughly 9M tokens and nearly two hours on LIBERO-Ultra-Long. Extending the budget adds more, concentrated in difficult episodes that often still fail: on RoboDojo, an extended-budget episode takes more than three hours on average. About 98% of tokens are cached input, so 1M tokens ≈ 1 USD . Inference latency is not counted in the step budget, so this cost also limits deployment where real-time control is required. Average per-task cost by benchmark Tokens (M) Time (min) Failure mode Verifying physical success GPT-6-Astra can tell a task is unfinished but not which physical condition is unmet, so its corrections fail to converge. Looking done, or reporting done, is not the same as meeting the task's contact, support and alignment conditions. Failure mode Recovering from consequential actions Each attempt changes the state that recovery starts from, and some changes cannot be undone . A failed prerequisite blocks every later subtask while retries drain the budget. Recovery works when GPT-6-Astra changes strategy rather than repeating itself, as in DexJoCo Fold Glasses, where a side approach and a test lift complete the task. ← Pour liquid into cup Multi-room navigation → Failure mode Preserving progress over long horizons Earlier progress must stay intact while later actions run, yet a later motion can undo it, and small errors in grasping, placement or navigation compound across stages . GPT-6-Astra has to keep rechecking what it has already done rather than treating completed subgoals as permanently resolved. Next 2 · Time & cost → 02 · Harness Ablation Harness Matters: An Ablation Token cost versus success rate on RoboDojo All A · System 1–System 2 B · Action interface 42 RoboDojo tasks; performance is the unweighted mean of category success rate. Dashed lines cross at the Agentic GPT-6-Astra baseline ; upper-left is better on both axes. Standalone VLA (π 0.5 , 6.91%) uses no GPT tokens and is not plotted. Hover a point to compare it with the baseline. A · System 1 – System 2 collaboration Supervision pays off, but every review costs tokens Letting the VLA run alone is insufficient; GPT-6-Astra reviewing its proposed actions works, but costs tokens. Reviewing four at a time saves 63.5% of tokens over per-action review, and adding ICL gives the best result — at about 6.9× the tokens of the best closed-loop setting without ICL. 5.83% open-loop 25.83% closed-loop · L = 4 54.17% ICL + VLA B · Action representation & chunking Interfaces should match how the model reasons Directional commands help and joint angles hurt. Letting the model choose its chunk size beats a fixed chunk in success rate, at a higher token cost. +2.50 directional −5.84 joint-angle +4.44 adaptive chunk 03 · Real-World Validation What Still Separates Benchmark Success from Deployment 01 / ZERO-SHOT No demonstrations, no knowledge package GPT-6-Astra performs as a generalist, without task- or robot-specific training. 02 / HUMAN PRIORS Structured context written by a human Tool schemas, joint limits, camera placement, safety constraints, hand presets and, on some platforms, task-level guidance such as admissible grasp points — no high-level semantic skills such as pick, place or insert. 03 / WALL CLOCK Budgeted in time, judged by a person Trials are normally limited to 60 minutes. An operator holds an emergency stop, and success is judged from the physical outcome, not the model's own claim. Embodiment # Main question Tasks Single arm, gripper Franka 3, Franka Panda, PiPER + Pika gripper 3 Do simulation results transfer, from rigid to deformable and precise tasks? Stacking and container nesting Cloth and towel folding Plug insertion Dual arm, grippers AgileX Piper 1 Can GPT-6-Astra coordinate two arms on harder zero-shot tasks? Ordered folding Flower insertion Bimanual holding Sorting Dual arm, dexterous hands Tianji M6S 1 Can GPT-6-Astra control high-DoF hands? Toy and bottle grasping Wheeled mobile manipulator Galaxea R1 Pro, AgileX Tracer + xArm7 2 Can GPT-6-Astra act over room-scale distances and long horizons? Find washer and press button Flower collection Tray arrangement Navigation and search Humanoid Unitree G1 1 Can GPT-6-Astra act as System 2 over low-level locomotion and arm control? Tabletop pick-and-drop Turn, approach and stop Findings and what changes in the real world ← 1 / 4 → 1 Finding One model, every embodiment 2 Finding Active vision 3 Finding System 2 over System 0 4 What changes Physical limits & missing demos Finding 1 One model drives every embodiment; success depends on the task Without platform-specific training, the same model controls all eight platforms. Rigid pick-and-place is reliable and matches simulation, whereas deformable objects, precise contact and long-horizon mobile tasks remain markedly harder. A second arm extends the range of zero-shot tasks, and GPT-6-Astra re-plans from execution feedback when the scene changes. Rigid pick-and-place stacking, nesting, toy grasps Deformable objects cloth folding on the Franka 3 Long-horizon mobile navigation & search, AgileX Tracer Precise contact plug insertion, three platforms Finding 2 What GPT-6-Astra can do depends on what it can see In flower insertion, the gripper holds the stem vertically, so its own wrist camera cannot see the vase mouth. On a single arm the insertion fails. On the dual-arm Piper, GPT-6-Astra moves the free arm until its wrist camera sees the vase mouth, then completes the insertion — the viewpoint becomes part of the action space. Teleoperated demonstrations rarely contain this active vision . Finding 3 GPT-6-Astra as System 2 over existing System 0 motor control On a real Unitree G1 with Wuji hands, GPT-6-Astra commands arm-joint targets and binary hand states for manipulation ( 2/3 ), and turns and walks through the vendor velocity interface ( 3/3 ) — without a task-trained System 1 policy. This establishes feasibility under slow, feedback-driven supervision rather than reliable real-time visuomotor control. What changes What changes in the real world In simulation, extra steps and failed attempts cost nothing, and demonstrations of the test task exist. On real robots neither holds: physical constraints limit extended execution, and missing demonstrations reshape in-context learning. Physical constraints Extended execution is not free on real hardware Extra steps and retries cost nothing in simulation. On real robots, protective stops and hardware faults end runs, and elapsed time adds tokens, risk, hardware stress and supervision. 2 / 3 PiPER plug-insertion trials ended by a joint collision fault 62 °C hand temperature guard ~90 % of G1 time deliberating Missing demonstrations Context quality decides the outcome Human-written context can stand in for demonstrations, but it is expert prompt engineering. Building context from other sources is an open problem. 0 / 3 Tianji grasps without grasp primitives 3 / 3 with human-written primitives 5 context sources untested Next 2 · Active vision → 04 · Prototype Towards a Next-Generation Embodied Benchmark 01 / HUMAN NEEDS Tasks derived from human needs Stated as a person would, e.g. “Could you make me breakfast?” Judged on the request ( Intent ) and on unstated obligations ( Duty ). 02 / NO DEMOS Experience acquired at test time No in-domain demonstrations. The agent learns the scene through its own exploration. 03 / WORLD CLOCK A world that keeps running Thinking takes world time, as on a real robot. The judge watches the whole trajectory, even after the agent says it is done. 1 Open-source assets publicly available obj

live_web_research.title: [2609.34261] RoboICL: Embodied In-Context Learning with GPT-6 ...
live_web_research.snippet: Sep 28, 2026 · General-purpose vision-language models offer a promising way to zero-shot robot control: \gptastra {} excels at open-ended and language- or image-conditioned manipulation but remains substantially weaker on high-precision and long-horizon tasks.
live_web_research.page_text: [2609.34261] RoboICL: Embodied In-Context Learning with GPT-6 Astra Skip to main content Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Robotics arXiv:2609.34261 (cs) [Submitted on 28 Sep 2026] Title: RoboICL: Embodied In-Context Learning with GPT-6 Astra Authors: Fangcheng Liu , Yeqing Shen , Anda Cheng , Weishi Mi , Chao Tang , Chenyuan Liu , Yushun Xiang , Tingguang Li , Yong-Lu Li , Yehui Tang View a PDF of the paper titled RoboICL: Embodied In-Context Learning with GPT-6 Astra, by Fangcheng Liu and 9 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: General-purpose vision-language models offer a promising way to zero-shot robot control: \gptastra{} excels at open-ended and language- or image-conditioned manipulation but remains substantially weaker on high-precision and long-horizon tasks. We introduce \emph{RoboICL}, an in-context robot-control framework that narrows these gaps without robot-specific parameter updates or a learned VLA. RoboICL separates \emph{demonstration context}, which provides recorded examples when available, from \emph{interaction memory}, which accumulates the model's own actions and observed outcomes. Both use a shared observation--action--receipt--observation grammar. To preserve experience across task stages, RoboICL combines sampled demonstration blocks with bounded anchored memory. Fixed anchors keep earlier rollout interactions available for in-context learning, while the latest interaction supports immediate error correction. Across 30 RoboDojo tasks, using zero shot for Open and one demonstration elsewhere, RoboICL improves on official zero-shot \gptastra{} by 20--27 progress-score points in every category. It leads the leaderboard baselines on Memory and Open, achieves comparable performance to the strongest Precision baseline, and remains competitive on Long-Horizon. Its 30-task Overall score is 50.64, versus 33.68 for the strongest baseline. On a separate ten-task subset, RoboICL scores 60.60, within 2.00 points of the $\pi_{0.5}$ + \gptastra{} hybrid approach. On three real-robot tasks, mean progress rises from 14.45 at zero shot to 63.33 at one shot and 78.89 at three shots. On two development tasks, optional Jev-gated action reuse reduces \gptastra{} calls by 33--48\%. Code is available at \href{ this https URL }{ this https URL }. live_web_research.snippet: Sep 17, 2026 · OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra achieves 95% success in robotic tasks, sparking debate on the future of embodied intelligence and data quality in robotics.
live_web_research.page_text: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra Revolutionizes Embodied Intelligence with High Success Rates - RobotToday Home Industry Briefing Now! Top News Humanoid News Research & Academics Drone and Military Company News CN News AP News Robotics Insights New Robotics Humanoids Industrial Robots Medical and Healthcare Robots Consumer and Service Robots Autonomous Vehicles and Drones Construction Robots Agriculture Robots Components and Hardware Miscellaneous Industry Trends Market and Business News Artificial Intelligence Innovations Research and Academia Standards and Regulations RobotToday Weekly Supplier Discovery Media Kit RSF Framework White Paper Reading List RSF Overview Events Calendar in Follow Search Subscribe Education & Research Robot Manufacturer Software & Algorithm Provider Human-Machine Interaction Motion & Navigation OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra Revolutionizes Embodied Intelligence with High Success Rates Published Sep 17, 2026 Source leaderobot.com in RobotToday Industry Briefing In early September, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra, which quickly gained attention for its ability to control robotic arms without additional training. Independent testing by Robocurve showed Astra achieving a 95% success rate in tasks involving dual-arm robots, significantly outperforming Claude Fable 5.1's 40%. This breakthrough has sparked discussions about the future of embodied intelligence, with experts divided on its implications. The significance of Astra's performance lies in its potential to reshape the robotics landscape. Zeeshan Zia, Chief Scientist at Amazon Alexa, suggested that OpenAI could dominate the robotics field, while others like He Yonghao, CTO of Virtual Time Technology, believe that traditional approaches may no longer hold value. The rapid advancements in language models are seen as a threat to embodied intelligence, with experts urging teams to accelerate their development. Looking ahead, the industry is keenly observing how Astra's capabilities will evolve. Some experts argue that while Astra excels in semantic and spatial generalization, it struggles with complex physical tasks. The ongoing debate highlights the importance of high-quality data in training models, with predictions that future iterations, like GPT-8, may focus on high-frequency motion control. No further timeline was disclosed at the time of publication. Editor's note The launch of GPT-6 Astra by OpenAI marks a pivotal moment in the robotics sector, particularly in embodied intelligence. As companies strive to integrate advanced AI capabilities into physical systems, the competition for high-quality training data and effective model architectures will intensify. Stakeholders must navigate the balance between cloud-based models and real-time processing to achieve optimal performance in robotic applications. article.body:
GPT-6-Astra’s benchmark gains do not establish practical robot autonomy

GPT-6-Astra was evaluated across 12 benchmarks covering tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms and dexterous hands. The report does not identify a specific robot body, joint count, gripper or payload, nor name particular objects manipulated. It also tested eight real-robot configurations, but the supplied report does not specify their environments or individual tasks.

For benchmark tests, GPT-6-Astra used in-context learning from training-set demonstrations, building a frozen package of task guidance and motion references; execution budgets reached 10 times the official limit. The control setup paired the model as a high-level reasoner with a low-level controller. Operator involvement is not specified.

The authors report costly demonstration collection and physical constraints on extending execution time. Their evidence supports benchmark competence and real-robot testing, not sustained practical capability.
